drills.los_text: discuss motivations to trade and how they relate to trading strategy

questions.stem: Motivations to trade are least likely to include:

options.A: risk management and hedging requirements.
options.B: profit seeking on an investment view.
options.C: soft-dollar commission generation.

rationales.A: Risk management and hedging needs are one of the four broad categories of motivations to trade. Trading arises when exposures drift away from target, when a hedge has to be added, reduced, or maintained, and when derivatives positions must be rolled or rebalanced.
rationales.B: Profit seeking is one of the four broad categories. Managers trade to capture expected alpha, whether from a short-term event-driven view traded with high urgency or from a longer-term fundamental view traded patiently over a long execution horizon.
rationales.C: Generating soft-dollar research commissions is not a motivation to trade. It is a conflict of interest to be managed and disclosed, because directing order flow in order to earn research credits can work against the duty of best execution; the trade itself still has to be justified by one of the genuine motivations. The four broad categories of motivations to trade are: (1) profit seeking, (2) risk management and hedging needs, (3) cash flow needs, and (4) corporate actions, index reconstitutions, and margin calls.

questions.stem: Trade urgency is most likely:

options.A: the number of counterparties used to fill an order.
options.B: the total notional value of the order.
options.C: how quickly or slowly an order is executed over the trading time horizon.

rationales.A: The number of counterparties or venues used to fill an order is an execution detail, not the dimension that urgency measures. Urgency is the time dimension of the trade strategy: a single counterparty can be worked patiently over a day, and many counterparties can be hit within seconds.
rationales.B: Notional value measures the size of the order; urgency measures its speed, that is, how quickly or slowly the order is executed over the trading horizon. The two are independent: a large order can be worked patiently over several days, and a small order can be executed aggressively within minutes.
rationales.C: Trade urgency refers to how quickly (aggressively) or slowly (patiently) the order is executed over the trading time horizon. Greater trade urgency is associated with executing over shorter execution horizons, whereas lower trade urgency is associated with executing over longer execution horizons. Urgency is driven by the expected rate of alpha decay, by market conditions, and by the risk aversion of the manager or trader.

questions.stem: Alpha decay in a trading context is most likely:

options.A: long-term underperformance by active managers.
options.B: erosion of short-term alpha once an investment decision is made.
options.C: the difference between benchmark and portfolio returns over a full year.

rationales.A: Persistent long-run underperformance by active managers is a separate empirical question about skill, fees, and market efficiency. Alpha decay is a short-horizon trading phenomenon: it describes how fast an identified opportunity disappears between decision and fill, not how a manager performs across years.
rationales.B: In a trading context, alpha decay refers to the erosion or deterioration in short-term alpha once an investment decision is made. A portfolio manager with a short-term event-driven strategy will trade with greater urgency if the expected alpha is likely to be rapidly acted on by other market participants; in that case the rate or level of expected alpha decay is high. Portfolio managers following a longer-term strategy based on company fundamentals will trade more patiently, with less urgency, when the rate or level of expected alpha decay is lower.
rationales.C: The difference between portfolio and benchmark returns over a period is active return, not alpha decay. Active return is a realized, after-the-fact measure of relative performance, whereas alpha decay describes how quickly expected alpha dissipates while an order is being worked.

questions.stem: During the period when the University of Michigan Index of Consumer Sentiment was distributed under a two-tiered release process, the speed with which S&P 500 Index prices incorporated the release is most likely best described as:

options.A: gradual, over the months that followed.
options.B: negligible, as the release had no measurable price impact.
options.C: immediate, within a fraction of a second.

rationales.A: Adjustment was not gradual. Under the two-tiered arrangement, paying subscribers received the sentiment reading ahead of the general public and traded on it at once, so the information was impounded into index prices essentially immediately. A months-long adjustment would imply the release carried information that nobody acted on.
rationales.B: Prices did adjust meaningfully to the release, so a claim of no market impact is wrong. The sentiment reading carries information about household consumption and the macroeconomic outlook, and S&P 500 Index prices moved on it as soon as the early-release subscribers were able to trade.
rationales.C: Hu, Pan, and Wang (2017) examined how quickly the information contained in the Index of Consumer Sentiment was incorporated into S&P 500 Index prices during the period of the two-tiered process, and found that most of the price adjustment happened within the first 200 milliseconds. This is an example of profit-driven trading with high associated trade urgency and an extremely short-term execution horizon: the expected alpha decays within a fraction of a second, so it can be captured only by executing immediately.

questions.stem: A value manager holding positions for months or years is most likely an example of:

options.A: profit seeking with low alpha decay and low trade urgency.
options.B: risk management and hedging needs.
options.C: profit seeking with high alpha decay and high trade urgency.

rationales.A: An investment manager following a value strategy attempts to identify undervalued companies, and to capitalize on those views individual positions may be held for months or years. Minimal trading is required, and any necessary trading can often be carried out in a more patient manner. Expected alpha decays slowly, because the mispricing is not expected to be competed away quickly, so trading in this case has no trade urgency and executions can be spread over much longer horizons to limit market impact.
rationales.B: The trade is motivated by the manager's return view, not by the need to add, reduce, or maintain a hedge. Risk management trades arise from changes in exposure, such as rebalancing a hedge, rolling derivatives, or cutting risk, which is a different motivation category from long-horizon profit seeking.
rationales.C: Value managers hold positions for months or years, so expected alpha decays slowly and trade urgency is low. High alpha decay paired with high urgency characterizes short-term event-driven strategies, where other market participants are expected to act on the same information within hours, or less.

questions.stem: For cash flow needs, urgency most likely:

options.A: is always high, regardless of the need.
options.B: varies with the nature of the need.
options.C: is always low, because cash needs can be anticipated.

rationales.A: A fund redemption driven by a longer-term change in client asset allocation settles on a schedule that permits patient execution, so urgency is not always high. Urgency varies with the deadline attached to the particular cash flow.
rationales.B: Cash flow needs may involve high or low trade urgency depending on their nature. Collateral and margin calls could require close-to-immediate liquidation, whereas a fund redemption due to longer-term client asset allocation changes might not require immediate liquidation. Fund inflows require capital to be invested and outflows require positions to be liquidated, but the horizon over which that trading is carried out depends on how quickly the cash is actually needed.
rationales.C: Collateral and margin calls demand near-immediate liquidation and are triggered by adverse market moves that cannot be reliably anticipated, so urgency is not uniformly low. Anticipation helps for scheduled redemptions, not for a call that must be met the same day.

questions.stem: Equitization is most likely:

options.A: a strategy for hedging the currency risk of foreign equity holdings.
options.B: a strategy for temporarily investing cash in futures or ETFs to gain equity exposure.
options.C: the tax equalization process applied to globally mobile employees.

rationales.A: The currency risk of foreign equity holdings is managed through a separate currency overlay, using forward or futures contracts on exchange rates. Equitization converts uninvested cash into equity exposure and leaves currency exposure untouched.
rationales.B: Equitization refers to a strategy of temporarily investing cash using futures or ETFs to gain the desired equity exposure before investing in the underlying securities longer term. It may be required if large inflows into a portfolio are hindered by lack of liquidity in the underlying securities. For example, a large inflow into a small-capitalization equity portfolio often cannot be invested immediately in the underlying stocks owing to limited market liquidity; instead, the manager may equitize the cash using equity futures or ETFs and then gradually trade into the underlying positions. The purpose is to minimize cash drag while the portfolio is being built.
rationales.C: Tax equalization for globally mobile employees is an unrelated compensation practice. In a portfolio trading context, equitization names the temporary market exposure taken on uninvested cash, not a tax process.

questions.stem: For hedge funds with lockup periods, redemptions most likely:

options.A: are made on a regular schedule, such as calendar quarter-ends.
options.B: are available daily without limitation.
options.C: are never permitted.

rationales.A: Hedge funds often have lockup periods in which fund redemptions are made according to a regular schedule, such as calendar quarter-ends. The stated objective is to protect remaining investors from incurring transaction charges resulting from other investors' redemption activity. These fund liquidations generally must be requested in advance, to allow fund managers time to trade out of potentially illiquid positions and thereby minimize trading costs.
rationales.B: Unlimited daily redemption describes a daily-liquidity vehicle such as a mutual fund or an ETF, not a fund with a lockup. The purpose of the lockup is precisely to restrict the dates on which capital can leave, so that illiquid positions need not be sold into the market on demand.
rationales.C: A lockup delays redemptions rather than prohibiting them. Capital can be withdrawn on the scheduled dates once the lockup period has expired, subject to the required advance notice.

questions.stem: For index tracking portfolios, when the index has additions, deletions, or constituent weight changes, the manager most likely:

options.A: trades the changes at the next day's opening auction.
options.B: trades the changes at the closing price.
options.C: trades the changes only at the open.

rationales.A: Waiting for the next day's opening auction leaves the portfolio misaligned with the benchmark overnight and adds tracking error: the benchmark reflects the new constituents and weights at the official close on the effective date, while the fund would still hold the old ones. Congestion in the closing auction is real, but that auction is also where index-change liquidity concentrates.
rationales.B: For index tracking portfolios, such index changes as additions, deletions, and constituent weight changes are generally traded in the manager's portfolio to reflect benchmark exposure. Since the fund's NAV is calculated using the official market close for each security, trading index changes at the closing price ensures that the same price is used for fund and benchmark valuation, which also uses the closing price in its calculation, and thus minimizes the fund's tracking error to the benchmark index.
rationales.C: Trading only at the open prices the fund's transition at a different point in the day from the benchmark, whose constituents change at the official close. Alignment with the close, not the open, is what minimizes tracking error.

drills.los_text: discuss inputs to the selection of a trading strategy

questions.stem: Inputs to the selection of a trade strategy are least likely to include:

options.A: the security's type, volatility, and liquidity.
options.B: the order's side, size, and relative size.
options.C: past benchmark-relative performance.

rationales.A: Security characteristics are one of the four key inputs: the security type (underlying security, ETF, ADR, or GDR), the expected short-term alpha, price volatility, and the security's liquidity all shape how aggressively the order can be worked.
rationales.B: Order characteristics are one of the four key inputs: the side of the trade (buy, sell, cover, or short), its absolute size, and its relative size as a percentage of average daily volume together determine the expected market impact and therefore the strategy.
rationales.C: The portfolio's past benchmark-relative performance is an outcome, not an input to trade strategy selection; it says nothing about how the order in hand should be executed. The key inputs for trade strategy selection are: (1) order characteristics, that is, side (buy, sell, cover, or short), size, and relative size as a percentage of average daily volume; (2) security characteristics, that is, type (underlying, ETF, ADR, or GDR), short-term alpha, price volatility, and security liquidity; (3) market conditions, including liquidity crises and other deviations from normal conditions; and (4) individual risk aversion, the willingness of the trader or manager to accept risk during trading.

questions.stem: Relative order size (% of ADV) is most likely:

options.A: Order size divided by the security's average daily volume.
options.B: Trade size in dollars.
options.C: Order size divided by the security's market capitalization.

rationales.A: Relative order size is the order size divided by the security's average daily volume (ADV), which makes order size comparable across securities. A 1 million share order in Stock ABC is not the same thing as a 1 million share order in Stock XYZ: if ABC has an average daily volume of 50 million shares, the order is 2% of ADV (1 million/50 million), while if XYZ has an average daily volume of 4 million shares, the same order is 25% of ADV (1 million/4 million). The larger the size of the trade expressed as a percentage of ADV, the larger the expected market impact cost.
rationales.B: Dollar size does not standardize across securities. The same dollar amount can be a trivial fraction of one security's daily turnover and a multiple of another's, so it says nothing about how hard the order will be to execute. Scaling the order by average daily volume is what makes the measure consistent across securities.
rationales.C: Relative order size is scaled by average daily volume, not by market capitalization. Trading volume, not firm size, determines the expected market impact of an order: a large-capitalization stock can trade thinly and a smaller-capitalization stock can trade heavily, so capitalization is a poor proxy for how much of a day's liquidity the order will consume.

questions.stem: Market impact is most likely:

options.A: The adverse price movement in a security caused by trading an order.
options.B: The difference between the decision price and the execution price.
options.C: The commissions and fees paid to execute an order.

rationales.A: Market impact is the adverse price movement in a security caused by trading an order, and it is one of the most significant costs in trading. Larger orders usually take longer to trade than smaller orders do, and portfolio managers will often trade larger orders in a more patient manner, with lower trade urgency, to reduce market impact. All else equal, trading larger order sizes more quickly will increase market impact cost, whereas trading smaller order sizes more slowly will decrease market impact cost.
rationales.B: The difference between the decision price and the execution price is implementation shortfall, a total cost measure. Market impact is only one of its components: implementation shortfall also captures delay cost, explicit commissions and fees, and, where the order is not completed, opportunity cost. Market impact is narrower, being the price pressure the order itself creates.
rationales.C: Commissions and fees are explicit costs, contracted and disclosed in advance. Market impact is an implicit cost, never invoiced and observable only as the adverse price movement the order causes while it is being worked. For institutional orders the implicit impact cost is typically the larger of the two.

questions.stem: Short-term alpha (or trading alpha) in a trading context is most likely:

options.A: The expected movement in security price over the trading horizon.
options.B: The long-term risk-adjusted excess return on the security.
options.C: The compensation earned by the portfolio manager.

rationales.A: Short-term alpha in a trading context is the expected movement in security price over the trading horizon, independent of the trade's own impact. Also called trading alpha or trade alpha, it may arise from an appreciation, a depreciation, or a reversion (that is, a reversal) in security price. Alpha decay results from price movement in the direction of the investment forecast and occurs regardless of whether the trade takes place, which is why expected short-term alpha is an input to the choice of trade urgency.
rationales.B: Long-term risk-adjusted excess return is classical alpha: return measured against a benchmark over an investment horizon. Short-term alpha is a trading concept measured over the much shorter trading horizon, and it is used to decide how quickly to execute rather than to judge investment skill.
rationales.C: Compensation is not alpha of any kind. Short-term alpha is the price movement expected over the trading horizon, an input to the trading strategy and to the urgency with which the order is worked, not a payment to the manager.

questions.stem: In an adversely trending market (buying in a rising market or selling in a falling market), portfolio managers most likely:

options.A: Make no adjustment to trade urgency.
options.B: Trade more patiently.
options.C: Trade at an accelerated rate.

rationales.A: The direction of the price trend is a direct input to trade urgency, so leaving urgency unchanged discards information the manager already has. In an adversely trending market, waiting is expected to be costly; in a favorably trending market, waiting is expected to pay. Neither case supports indifference to the trend.
rationales.B: Trading more patiently is the appropriate response to a favorably trending market, such as buying in a falling market or selling in a rising market, where more favorable prices are expected later in the trading horizon. In an adversely trending market, patience means executing at the less favorable prices expected later.
rationales.C: In an adversely trending market, for example buying in a rising market or selling in a falling market, portfolio managers may trade at an accelerated rate if less favorable prices are expected later in the trading horizon; accelerating captures prices before they move further against the order. In a favorably trending market, for example buying in a falling market or selling in a rising market, portfolio managers are better off trading more slowly to execute at the more favorable prices expected later in the trading horizon. The cost of accelerating is greater market impact, which the expected adverse price trend has to outweigh.

questions.stem: Execution risk is most likely:

options.A: The risk of an adverse price movement over the trading horizon.
options.B: The risk that a completed trade fails to settle.
options.C: The same concept as market impact cost.

rationales.A: Execution risk is the risk of an adverse price movement occurring over the trading horizon, owing either to a change in the fundamental value of the security or to trading-induced volatility. It is often proxied by price volatility: securities with higher levels of price volatility have greater exposure to execution risk than securities with lower price volatility. That is why higher-volatility names are generally worked with greater trade urgency, accepting more market impact in exchange for less exposure to price movement.
rationales.B: Failure of a completed trade to settle is settlement or operational risk, which arises after execution in the clearing and settlement process. Execution risk concerns price movement during the trading horizon, while the order is still being worked.
rationales.C: Market impact is the adverse price movement the trader's own order causes through its buying or selling pressure and its information content. Execution risk is the risk of adverse price movement over the trading horizon arising from changes in the security's fundamental value or from trading-induced volatility, and it is proxied by price volatility rather than by order size relative to average daily volume. The two move in opposite directions as urgency changes: trading faster reduces execution risk and raises market impact.

questions.stem: A high level of individual risk aversion in a trader most likely results in:

options.A: Lower trade urgency.
options.B: No change in trade urgency.
options.C: Higher trade urgency.

rationales.A: Patient execution with lower trade urgency is the low-risk-aversion posture. A trader who is more concerned about market risk shortens the time the order is exposed to the market by trading quickly, so a high level of risk aversion raises urgency rather than lowering it.
rationales.B: Risk aversion is a direct input to the choice of trading strategy, alongside order size relative to average daily volume, security volatility and expected short-term alpha. A trader with high risk aversion is more concerned about market risk and trades with greater urgency to cut exposure to execution risk, so the strategy is not independent of risk aversion.
rationales.C: A portfolio manager or trader with a high level of risk aversion is likely to be more concerned about market risk and will tend to trade with greater trade urgency to avoid the greater market exposure associated with trading more patiently. A portfolio manager with a low level of risk aversion might be less concerned about market risk and may tend to trade more patiently, or more passively, with lower levels of trade urgency. The trade-off is that greater urgency reduces exposure to adverse price movement over the trading horizon at the cost of higher market impact.

questions.stem: Compared with permanent market impact, temporary market impact is most likely:

options.A: Longer lasting.
options.B: Identical to permanent impact.
options.C: Short lived and subsequently reversed.

rationales.A: The two components differ in duration in the opposite direction. The temporary component is the short-lived price effect of the order's buying or selling pressure, which reverses once the order is complete, while the permanent component is the part of the price change that persists.
rationales.B: The two components differ in both cause and duration. Temporary impact arises from the immediate need to buy or sell and reverses afterward; permanent impact arises from the information the trade conveys to other market participants and does not reverse. Separating them matters because only the permanent component represents a lasting repricing of the security.
rationales.C: The temporary market impact cost of trading an order is the often short-lived impact on security price from trading to meet the need to buy or sell. Post-trade prices should revert, with prices decreasing after completion of a buy order and increasing after completion of a sell order. The permanent component of the price change associated with trading an order is the market price impact caused by the information content of the trade: trading in the market often conveys information to other participants that the asset may be under- or overvalued, so they adjust their own valuations and that part of the price change persists.

questions.stem: The four categories of reference price benchmarks used in evaluating trade execution most likely are:

options.A: Pre-trade, intraday, post-trade, and market-adjusted.
options.B: Decision price, arrival price, VWAP, and closing price.
options.C: Pre-trade, intraday, post-trade, and price target.

rationales.A: Market-adjusted benchmarks are not one of the four categories. The fourth category is price target benchmarks, whose reference price is a specified price to meet or beat. Adjusting a measured cost for general market movement is a refinement applied to a benchmark such as arrival price, not a benchmark category in its own right.
rationales.B: Decision price, arrival price, VWAP and the closing price are individual reference prices drawn from three of the categories rather than the categories themselves: decision price and arrival price are pre-trade benchmarks, VWAP is an intraday benchmark, and the closing price is a post-trade benchmark. The four categories are pre-trade, intraday, post-trade and price target.
rationales.C: The four categories are: (1) pre-trade benchmarks, whose reference price is known before the start of trading, including decision price, previous close, opening price and arrival price; (2) intraday benchmarks, based on prices observed during the trading period, such as VWAP and TWAP; (3) post-trade benchmarks, whose reference price is determined at the end of trading, such as the closing price; and (4) price target benchmarks, whose reference price is a specified price to meet or beat.

questions.stem: The decision price benchmark is most likely:

options.A: The security's closing price on the day of the trade.
options.B: The security price when the manager decided to trade.
options.C: The volume-weighted average price over the trading day.

rationales.A: The closing price is itself a reference price, but a post-trade one, determined at the end of trading. The decision price is struck earlier, at the moment the portfolio manager decides to buy or sell, which makes it a pre-trade benchmark.
rationales.B: The decision price benchmark represents the security price at the time the portfolio manager made the decision to buy or sell the security. In many situations portfolio managers have exact records of the price at which they decided to trade, and quantitative portfolio managers will often have such records because these prices may be inputs into their quantitative models. Measuring cost against the decision price captures delay cost, the price drift between the decision and the order reaching the market, as well as the cost of execution itself.
rationales.C: The volume-weighted average price over the trading day is a separate intraday benchmark, computed from the prices and volumes observed while the order is being worked. The decision price anchors cost to the moment of the investment decision, before any trading has begun.

questions.stem: The arrival price benchmark is most likely:

options.A: The security's previous closing price.
options.B: The average of intraday prices.
options.C: The security price when the order is entered into the market.

rationales.A: The previous close is a different pre-trade benchmark, set before the trading day begins and therefore unaffected by any overnight news or by the opening auction. The arrival price is struck later, when the order reaches the market for execution.
rationales.B: An average of intraday prices is VWAP or TWAP, an intraday benchmark measured across the whole trading period. The arrival price is a single point-in-time price, captured at the moment the order is entered for execution.
rationales.C: The arrival price is the price of the security at the time the order is entered into the market for execution. Portfolio managers who are buying or selling on the basis of alpha expectations or a current market mispricing will often specify an arrival price benchmark, because their goal is to transact at or close to current market prices in order to complete execution and realize as much potential alpha as possible. Portfolio managers looking to minimize trading cost will also in many cases specify the arrival price as their benchmark.

questions.stem: VWAP is most likely:

options.A: The last trade price of the day.
options.B: The average of the day's high and low prices.
options.C: The volume-weighted average price of all trades over the day.

rationales.A: The last price of the day is the closing price, a separate reference price. A closing price benchmark is typically chosen by index managers and mutual funds whose holdings are valued at the official market close, and it says nothing about the volume traded at each price during the session.
rationales.B: The midpoint of the day's high and low weights neither volume nor time and reflects only two extreme prints. VWAP weights every execution by the number of shares traded at that price, so the prices at which heavy volume occurred dominate the average.
rationales.C: The VWAP benchmark price is the volume-weighted average price of all trades executed over the day or the trading horizon. Portfolio managers may specify a VWAP benchmark when they wish to participate with volume patterns over the day. Managers who are rebalancing a portfolio over the day and have both buy and sell orders may also select VWAP as the price benchmark; exposure to market risk is reduced by a two-sided (buy/sell) trade list worked over the same horizon.

questions.stem: TWAP is most likely:

options.A: The same measure as VWAP under a different name.
options.B: The equal-weighted average price of trades over the horizon.
options.C: The volume-weighted average price of trades over the horizon.

rationales.A: VWAP and TWAP are structurally different measures, not two vendor names for one calculation. VWAP weights each execution by the volume traded at that price, while TWAP weights each trade, and so each time slice, equally.
rationales.B: The TWAP benchmark price is the equal-weighted average price of all trades executed over the day or trading horizon. Unlike VWAP, TWAP does not consider volume traded and is simply the average price of trades executed over the specified time horizon. Portfolio managers may choose TWAP when they wish to exclude potential trade outliers, which arise from trading a large buy order at the day's low or a large sell order at the day's high; because volume is ignored, those heavily traded extreme prints cannot dominate the benchmark.
rationales.C: Volume weighting is what defines VWAP. TWAP is the equal-weighted average and ignores volume entirely, which is precisely the feature that keeps large outlier trades from pulling the benchmark price toward the day's low or high.

questions.stem: The closing price benchmark is most likely used by:

options.A: Index managers and mutual funds valued at the official close.
options.B: Intraday day traders.
options.C: High-turnover quantitative funds.

rationales.A: The closing price is typically used by index managers and mutual funds that wish to execute transactions at the closing price for the day. For managers with index mandates, the fund's securities are themselves valued using the official market close for each security, so it is important to know how close executions are to a benchmark price that also uses the official market close in its calculation. A manager who is managing tracking error to a benchmark will generally select a closing price benchmark, since the closing price is the price used to compute the fund's valuation.
rationales.B: Day traders typically close their positions before the end of the session and are not valued at the official close, so the closing price is not their natural reference. Index managers and mutual funds valued at the close are, and no one group uses the benchmark exclusively.
rationales.C: Quantitative funds generally benchmark to the decision price or the arrival price, because the question that matters to them is how much of the signal captured at the moment of the decision survives implementation. Minimizing tracking error against a close-valued benchmark is the index manager's and the mutual fund's concern.

questions.stem: The opening price benchmark is most likely preferred over previous close or decision price because:

options.A: It is the price used to calculate the fund's NAV.
options.B: It carries no overnight risk.
options.C: It is easier to obtain.

rationales.A: The closing price, not the opening price, is the price used for fund NAV calculation. That is the argument for a closing price benchmark and the tracking-error minimization it provides, not an argument for the opening price benchmark.
rationales.B: Portfolio managers may choose an opening price instead of the decision price or the previous close because, unlike a reference price from the prior day or earlier, the opening price does not have associated overnight risk, the risk that prices will adjust at the market open to incorporate information released after the close of the previous business day. The opening price cannot serve as the benchmark if the trade is executed in the opening auction itself, since the trade would then set its own benchmark.
rationales.C: All three reference prices are equally observable, so ease of obtaining the price does not distinguish them. The opening price's advantage is the removal of overnight risk.

questions.stem: The price target benchmark is most likely:

options.A: The arrival price when the order reaches the market.
options.B: The price the manager specifies to meet or beat.
options.C: The volume-weighted average price over the trade horizon.

rationales.A: The arrival price is a pre-trade benchmark: the market price at the moment the order is released to the market. A price target benchmark instead reflects the manager's perceived fair value of the security, which may sit well away from the prevailing market price.
rationales.B: Portfolio managers seeking short-term alpha may select a price target benchmark, which specifies a price to meet or beat, meaning to transact more favorably than. A manager who believes a stock trading at $20.00 is undervalued by $0.50 will seek to purchase shares by specifying a price target of $20.50 or better, with better meaning lower than $20.50 in the case of a buy. The benchmark price is the perceived fair value price of $20.50.
rationales.C: VWAP is an intraday benchmark computed from market activity during the trading period, so the market determines it rather than the manager. A price target benchmark is a manager-specified price to meet or beat.

questions.stem: The main disadvantage of the closing price benchmark is most likely:

options.A: It is subject to overnight risk.
options.B: It is not known until trading is completed.
options.C: It cannot be used for funds valued at NAV.

rationales.A: The closing price benchmark uses the current day's close, so no overnight period separates the benchmark from the trading it measures. Overnight risk is the drawback of a previous-close reference price, and avoiding it is one reason a manager may prefer an opening price benchmark.
rationales.B: An advantage of the closing price benchmark is that it provides portfolio managers with the price used for fund valuation and thus minimizes potential tracking error. The disadvantage is that the benchmark price is not known until after trading is completed, so portfolio managers have no way of knowing whether they are performing more or less favorably relative to the benchmark until the trading is done.
rationales.C: The closing price is precisely the price used for NAV-based fund valuation, so it can certainly be used for such funds. That match is the benchmark's main advantage, since it minimizes potential tracking error.

drills.los_text: recommend and justify a trading strategy (given relevant facts)

questions.stem: XYZ is trading at a significant discount in the pre-market that the manager believes is an overreaction, and the order therefore carries high trade urgency. The most appropriate trading strategy is most likely to:

options.A: Trade part of the order in the opening auction and the residual in the open market.
options.B: Trade the entire order in the closing auction.
options.C: Trade the order passively across the day through dark pools.

rationales.A: Given the possibility of short-term price increases in XYZ, this order has associated trade urgency, and the trader does not have the benefit of trading it passively, as with a VWAP or TWAP participation strategy, since XYZ's price could rise to fair value at any time. The trader will likely want to trade a portion of the order in the opening auction and then continue trading any residual in the open market, working against a price target benchmark such as a $60 limit. Dark pool venues would be avoided here, given their greater risk of unfilled executions if offsetting orders do not arrive.
rationales.B: Waiting for the closing auction leaves the order unexecuted through the session in which the price is most likely to correct toward fair value, forfeiting the overreaction opportunity. The urgency argues for the opening auction with an open-market residual worked against a price target or limit.
rationales.C: A passive full-day VWAP or TWAP schedule is the strategy for a low-urgency order, and it surrenders the short-term alpha that the pre-market discount offers. Routing to dark pools compounds the problem by adding the risk of unfilled executions if offsetting orders do not arrive.

questions.stem: For a fixed-income order driven by a long-term alpha view with low trade urgency, the most appropriate strategy is most likely to:

options.A: Trade patiently over an extended horizon through broker agency executions.
options.B: Trade the order in the closing auction.
options.C: Trade the entire order at the open.

rationales.A: Longer-term alpha-driven strategies, such as value investing or long-term fixed-income mandates, have low trade urgency, so managers trade patiently and spread executions over longer horizons to capture favorable prices. In fixed-income markets, and particularly in illiquid corporate bonds, large non-urgent trades are generally implemented via broker agency trades, with the broker acting as agent to source liquidity rather than taking the other side as principal. This provides more favorable execution over a longer period, but it requires patience.
rationales.B: The closing auction serves trades that must be priced off the official close, such as index and NAV-related flows. A long-term alpha view neither needs the closing price nor benefits from concentrating the whole order into a single auction.
rationales.C: Trading the full order at the open concentrates execution into one moment and pays market impact that a low-urgency, long-horizon view does not require; long-term views do not call for that urgency.

questions.stem: A macro hedge fund with a balanced list of buys and sells wishes to lower the portfolio's volatility, and the portfolio is not in breach of its guidelines. The most appropriate trading strategy is most likely:

options.A: A single trade at the market open.
options.B: An aggressive full-day strategy using dark pools only.
options.C: A TWAP algorithm over the next day or two.

rationales.A: A single trade concentrates the entire rebalance into one moment and pays the market impact of that concentration. Since the portfolio is not in breach of its guidelines, there is no need to accept that cost.
rationales.B: Aggressive execution does not match a controlled and gradual reduction of risk, and restricting the order to dark pools adds the risk of unfilled executions, which would break the hedge between the buy and sell sides.
rationales.C: Since the portfolio is not in breach of its guidelines and the portfolio manager wishes to reduce risk on a controlled and gradual basis, the trader can trade the order passively to lower the fund's risk level. Using a TWAP reference price for the trade and a TWAP algorithm to execute over the next day or two, or longer depending on the size of the position, is an appropriate trading strategy. By trading all the orders over the same trading horizon with a TWAP strategy, the trader maintains the hedge that exists between the buys and the sells, which helps reduce execution risk.

questions.stem: A client redeeming from the fund will receive the fund's NAV calculated at the close. The most appropriate trading strategy is most likely to:

options.A: Trade the order at the market open.
options.B: Send the order to the closing auction.
options.C: Trade through the day against an arrival price benchmark.

rationales.A: The market open does not match NAV pricing. Executing at the open leaves the trader bearing the full difference between the execution prices and the closing prices used to calculate the fund's NAV.
rationales.B: The client will receive the NAV of the fund regardless of how well or poorly the trader executes, so the trader bears the risk of executing at any price other than the closing price unless each position can be guaranteed at that price. A closing price reference price is therefore most appropriate. On exchanges such as NASDAQ, NYSE, TSE, Deutsche Börse (Xetra) and HKEX, the trader can send the order to the closing auction and receive the auction-guaranteed closing price on all orders submitted to the auction. If the order is large relative to closing auction volume, the trader may split it, for example sending 90% to the close and working 10% with a VWAP strategy during the day.
rationales.C: An arrival price references the market price when the order reaches the market, which bears no relation to the closing price used to calculate NAV, so the trader would remain exposed to the difference.

questions.stem: A trader must invest a new €100 million mandate in the MDAX, subject to a 3% tracking error limit, with performance measured from today's close. The most appropriate implementation strategy is most likely:

options.A: An indefinite cash holding until entry prices improve.
options.B: Gradual purchases of the underlying stocks, with no interim exposure.
options.C: Immediate MDAX futures exposure, unwound as the stocks are bought.

rationales.A: Holding cash against an equity benchmark is the one guaranteed way to trail it: any rise in the MDAX is an immediate shortfall, and the shortfall is measured from today's close. Waiting for attractive entry prices is also a market-timing decision the mandate does not call for. Cash drag is the cost the trader can remove on day one, and futures equitization removes it immediately.
rationales.B: Buying the underlying stocks over many days leaves the mandate underexposed to the MDAX for as long as the build takes. Because performance measurement begins at today's close, any index rise during that period is an immediate shortfall against the benchmark, and the 3% tracking error budget is consumed by missing exposure rather than by deliberate active positions.
rationales.C: The trader can obtain more immediate exposure by buying €100 million worth of MDAX futures traded on Eurex, a major European derivatives exchange. After establishing that initial exposure, the trader begins building the underlying stock positions over time and unwinds the equivalent futures exposure as the stock is acquired. This allows the mandate to achieve full €100 million exposure to the MDAX from the outset, eliminating the opportunity cost of holding cash balances relative to the benchmark. For smaller mandates in liquid securities, the equitization-via-futures step may be skipped and the stocks bought directly.

questions.stem: For a trade list of buys and sells with a net beta of approximately zero, trade urgency relative to a directional trade is most likely:

options.A: Not relevant.
options.B: Lower.
options.C: Greater.

rationales.A: Trade urgency does not disappear for a balanced list. It still has to be assessed against volatility, order size, and the manager's motivation to trade. What changes is its level, not its relevance: because the buys and sells offset one another in market risk exposure, urgency is lower than for a directional trade rather than absent.
rationales.B: Although volatility may have increased significantly, the risk exposure of the trade is more limited if the list of buys and sells is balanced in market risk exposure, such as a buy/sell trade list with a net beta of approximately zero. The offsetting positions leave little exposure to a general market move, so the trader does not have the same trade urgency as on a trade with a positive or negative net beta, such as one containing all buys or all sells, which might involve significantly more risk arising from exposure to potential market movement. Risk-averse market participants typically have greater trade urgency for trades with directional market exposure than for trades that are balanced, or hedged, in market exposure.
rationales.C: This reverses the relationship. Directional trades, those carrying a positive or negative net beta, are the ones exposed to a general market move and therefore carry greater urgency. A list balanced in market exposure carries less market risk, and so less urgency, not more.

questions.stem: The share of a day's total trading volume that the US opening auction typically represents is most likely:

options.B: More than 30%.

rationales.A: The opening auction is a small fraction of the trading day, not half of it. At 50% of daily volume, an order equal to 2% of expected volume could be sent into the auction without dominating it, which is the opposite of the sizing constraint traders actually face at the open.
rationales.B: More than 30% overstates auction volume by more than an order of magnitude. Opening auctions are much smaller than continuous trading, which is precisely why auction submissions have to be sized against expected auction volume rather than against the full day.
rationales.C: Research shows the US opening auction typically makes up between 1% and 1.25% of a day's volume. An order representing approximately 2% of expected daily volume would therefore be roughly the entire auction if it were submitted in full, so a trader would not likely place the full order into the opening auction. Managers must size opening auction submissions relative to expected auction volume, not relative to the day's volume.

questions.stem: For a sell order that is large relative to expected liquidity in the closing auction, the most appropriate approach is most likely:

options.A: Cancellation of the order.
options.B: Partial execution in the market before the close, with the remainder in the auction.
options.C: Execution of the entire order in the closing auction.

rationales.A: Cancelling abandons the portfolio manager's investment decision rather than managing its implementation, and leaves the client holding an unwanted position. The impact concern is handled by splitting the order, for example trading 10% of it at VWAP in the market up to the close and sending the remaining 90% to the closing auction.
rationales.B: From a fiduciary standpoint, trading in a manner that will lead to a poorer execution for a client is inappropriate. When trades are large relative to expected liquidity in the closing auction, the approach portfolio managers follow is to execute both in the market and in the closing auction: identify a reasonable amount to send to the auction, say 90% of the order, trade the order remainder in the market prior to the close of trading, say 10% of the order at VWAP up to the close, and then send the identified 90% to the closing auction. Some brokers offer close algorithms that automate this split.
rationales.C: Concentrating the whole order in the closing auction is exactly what creates the adverse impact on the closing price, and therefore on NAV, because the order is large relative to the liquidity the auction can absorb. Splitting the order between the market before the close and the auction limits that impact.

questions.curriculum_ref: Trading Strategies — split close vs VWAP

questions.stem: The primary goal of any trading strategy is most likely to:

options.A: balance the expected costs and risks of trading the order.
options.B: trade at the fastest achievable speed.
options.C: execute at the lowest possible price.

rationales.A: The primary goal of any trading strategy is to balance the expected costs and risks associated with trading the order in the market consistent with the portfolio manager's trading objectives, risk aversion, and other known constraints. A portfolio manager's motivation to trade, risk aversion, and trade urgency for the order, together with other factors such as order size and market conditions at the time of trading, are thus key in determining an appropriate trade strategy.
rationales.B: Maximum speed minimizes execution risk but maximizes market impact cost, so it optimizes only one side of the trade-off. The objective balances the two, consistent with the manager's trading objectives and risk aversion; high speed is appropriate only where trade urgency is genuinely high.
rationales.C: The lowest possible price is rarely achievable, and chasing it means delaying execution, which raises execution risk and opportunity cost. Price is one input into the cost side of a strategy that must balance expected cost against risk, not the goal in itself.

drills.los_text: describe factors that typically determine the selection of a trading algorithm class

questions.stem: The two primary purposes of trading algorithms are most likely:

options.A: Trade execution and profit generation.
options.B: Market making and settlement optimization.
options.C: Trade execution and regulatory reporting.

rationales.A: Trading algorithms are primarily used for two purposes: trade execution and profit generation. Execution algorithms transact the investment decisions already made by the portfolio manager. Profit-seeking algorithms both determine what to buy or sell and then implement those decisions efficiently; they are used by electronic market makers, quantitative funds, and high-frequency traders.
rationales.B: Market making is only one specific case of profit seeking, carried out by electronic market makers running profit-seeking algorithms, so it is too narrow to stand as one of the two primary purposes. Settlement optimization is a post-trade operational activity and not an algorithm purpose at all. The two primary purposes are trade execution and profit generation.
rationales.C: Trade execution is one of the two, but regulatory reporting is a compliance function rather than a purpose of a trading algorithm. The second primary purpose is profit generation, pursued by the profit-seeking algorithms of electronic market makers, quantitative funds, and high-frequency traders.

questions.stem: Scheduled algorithms, such as POV, VWAP, and TWAP algorithms, most likely send orders to the market following:

options.A: A schedule determined by historical volumes or specified time periods.
options.B: A schedule confined to the market open and close.
options.C: A randomized schedule intended to avoid detection.

rationales.A: Scheduled algorithms send orders to the market following a schedule that is determined by historical volumes or specified time periods. They include percentage of volume (POV) algorithms, volume-weighted average price algorithms, and time-weighted average price algorithms. POV algorithms, also known as participation algorithms, send orders following a volume participation schedule, such as a 10% participation rate; as trading volume increases in the market, these algorithms trade more shares. VWAP and TWAP algorithms release orders to the market following a time-specified schedule.
rationales.B: POV, VWAP, and TWAP algorithms work through the trading day according to their volume participation or time schedules, not only in the opening and closing auctions. Restricting execution to the open and close is an auction-targeting strategy, and it would defeat the purpose of a schedule designed to spread an order over a trading horizon.
rationales.C: Randomization is an anti-gaming overlay applied on top of other strategies, not the basis of a scheduled algorithm. Scheduled algorithms follow either a volume schedule or a time schedule, both of which are deliberately structured rather than random.

questions.stem: A POV algorithm specified with a 10% participation rate most likely executes:

options.A: 10% of the order in the opening auction.
options.B: 1,000 shares for every 10,000 shares traded in the market.
options.C: 10% of the order during the first hour of trading.

rationales.A: A participation rate does not front-load the order into the opening auction. The 10% refers to the algorithm's share of market volume over the life of the order, so execution is spread across the trading period in proportion to volume rather than concentrated at the open.
rationales.B: Investors specify the POV algorithm through the participation rate, which determines the volume participation strategy. A participation rate of 10% indicates that the algorithm will participate with 10% of the market volume until the order is completed. In this case, for every 10,000 shares that trade in the market, the algorithm will execute 1,000 shares. The advantage is that the algorithm automatically takes advantage of increased liquidity; the disadvantage is that it may not complete the order within a specified time period.
rationales.C: The 10% is a share of market volume, not a share of the order to be completed within the first hour. Participation continues at 10% of market volume throughout the trading period until the order is filled, so how long the order takes depends on how much volume trades.

questions.stem: Liquidity-seeking algorithms are most likely appropriate for:

options.A: Small orders only, and only in liquid markets.
options.B: Small orders requiring immediate execution.
options.C: Large orders requiring quick execution without substantial price impact.

rationales.A: Liquidity-seeking algorithms exist to source size that is not displayed, so confining them to small orders in liquid markets removes their reason for being. They are in fact appropriate for large orders, and also for securities that are relatively less liquid and thinly traded or where liquidity is episodic.
rationales.B: Immediacy on a small order is better served by taking the displayed quote, since a small order is unlikely to move the price or to leak information. Liquidity-seeking algorithms address the large-order problem of executing quickly without signaling trading intentions, which is not the small-order case.
rationales.C: Liquidity-seeking algorithms are appropriate for large orders that the portfolio manager or trader would like to execute quickly without having a substantial impact on the security price. They are also used when displaying sizable liquidity via limit orders could lead to unwanted information leakage and adverse security price movement; in those cases the priority is to minimize information leakage associated with order execution and avoid signaling the trading intentions of the portfolio manager or trader to the market. They are appropriate as well for trading securities that are relatively less liquid and thinly traded, or when liquidity is episodic, with thin order books interrupted by occasional tight spreads and thick books.

questions.stem: Arrival price algorithms are most likely:

options.A: Spread uniformly across the entire trading day.
options.B: Front-loaded toward the beginning of trading.
options.C: Concentrated at the end of the trading day.

rationales.A: Spreading execution uniformly over the day is the TWAP profile. An arrival price algorithm benchmarks to the price prevailing when the order was received, so holding back an even share of the order all day leaves the execution exposed to drift away from that benchmark.
rationales.B: Arrival price algorithms seek to trade close to current market prices at the time the order is received for execution. They trade more aggressively at the beginning of trading in order to execute more shares nearer to the arrival price, which is known as a front-loaded strategy. Arrival price algorithms tend to be time schedule based but can also be volume participation based. They are used for orders in which the portfolio manager or trader believes prices are likely to move unfavorably during the trade horizon, or where the trader is risk averse and wishes to reduce execution risk, and they suit orders that are not outsized, generally less than 15% of expected volume.
rationales.C: Concentrating trading at the end of the day maximizes the time over which the price can drift from the arrival price, the opposite of the algorithm's objective. End-of-day concentration serves a closing-price benchmark, not an arrival price benchmark.

questions.stem: Dark aggregator algorithms are most likely appropriate for:

options.A: trades requiring immediate, certain execution.
options.B: large orders at risk of impact and information leakage.
options.C: small orders in highly liquid securities.

rationales.A: Dark venues offer less certainty of execution, because offsetting orders may never arrive. An order that must be filled immediately and with certainty therefore belongs in lit markets, where displayed liquidity can be taken at once.
rationales.B: Dark aggregator algorithms are used when portfolio managers and traders are concerned about information leakage that may occur from posting limit orders in lit venues with pre- and post-trade transparency. They are used when order size is large relative to the market, meaning a large percentage of expected volume, and when trading in the open market using arrival price or VWAP strategies would lead to significant market impact. They are also appropriate for trading securities that are relatively illiquid or that have relatively wide bid-ask spreads. Since trading in dark pools offers less certainty of execution, as offsetting orders may never arrive, these algorithms are appropriate for trades in which the trader or portfolio manager does not need to execute the order in its entirety.
rationales.C: Small orders in highly liquid securities route efficiently through lit markets using direct market access or a smart order router. They generate little market impact, so the execution uncertainty of a dark venue buys nothing.

questions.stem: Smart order routers (SORs) most likely:

options.A: execute exclusively in dark pools, never in lit venues.
options.B: send every order to a single pre-designated venue.
options.C: route each order to the best available venue.

rationales.A: Smart order routers span lit and dark destinations. They continuously monitor real-time data from exchanges and venues and also assess ongoing activity in dark pools, so they are not confined to dark pools.
rationales.B: The router's function is venue choice, not a fixed destination. For a limit order it determines the destination with the highest probability of execution, and for a market order the venue with the best market price; both of those change with prevailing market conditions, so no single venue can be designated in advance.
rationales.C: Smart order routers determine how best to route an order given prevailing market conditions. The SOR determines the destination with the highest probability of executing a limit order, and the venue with the best market price for a market order, known in the United States as the National Best Bid and Offer (NBBO). The SOR continuously monitors real-time data from exchanges and venues and also assesses ongoing activity in dark pools. SORs are used when a portfolio manager or trader wishes to execute a small order.

questions.stem: A portfolio manager with a moderate-size order in a liquid stock expects short-term buying pressure from other participants into the market close. The most appropriate algorithm for the order is most likely:

options.A: a dark aggregator algorithm.
options.B: an arrival price algorithm.
options.C: a closing auction order.

rationales.A: Dark aggregators are best suited to orders that are large relative to expected volume and to relatively illiquid securities. The order here is moderate in size and the stock is liquid, so that treatment is unnecessary, and the low execution certainty of dark venues would leave the manager still exposed to the adverse prices expected later in the day.
rationales.B: An arrival price algorithm is most appropriate for trading this order because the portfolio manager has adverse price expectations. In this case, the portfolio manager wants to trade more aggressively to capture alpha ahead of less favorable prices expected later in the day. By trading the order more quickly, the portfolio manager can execute at more favorable prices ahead of the adverse price movement and ahead of the less favorable prices expected from other participants' buying pressure into the close, in line with his trade urgency.
rationales.C: A closing auction defers the whole execution to the close, which is exactly when the other participants' buying pressure is expected to have moved the price against the manager. It would lock in the adverse price rather than trade ahead of it.

drills.los_text: contrast key characteristics of the following markets in relation to trade implementation: equity, fixed income, options and futures, OTC derivatives, and spot currency

questions.stem: Equity markets are most likely characterized by:

options.A: high transparency with pre- and post-trade information.
options.B: an OTC dealer market with little transparency.
options.C: pre-trade transparency with no post-trade reporting.

rationales.A: Equity markets are highly electronically traded, with both pre-trade information, in the form of displayed quotes and depth of book, and post-trade information, in the form of reported trade prices and volumes, available on lit venues. Algorithmic and electronic trading is well established: small trades often use direct market access or smart order routers, while larger trades use algorithms such as VWAP, TWAP, percentage of volume, arrival price and dark aggregators. This is in stark contrast to less liquid markets.
rationales.B: A bilateral, dealer-centric structure with quotes provided only on request describes fixed-income markets more than equity markets. Equities trade on exchanges and other lit venues with continuous displayed quotes rather than principally through dealers.
rationales.C: Lit equity venues provide both halves of transparency. Pre-trade, quotes and depth of book are displayed; post-trade, trade prices and volumes are reported. The absence of post-trade reporting is therefore wrong.

questions.stem: Fixed-income markets are most likely characterized by:

options.A: a bilateral, dealer-centric structure with quotes on request.
options.B: high transparency and fully electronic trading of all bonds.
options.C: a structure identical to that of equity markets.

rationales.A: Fixed-income securities are generally traded in a bilateral, dealer-centric market structure. Investors will generally get quotes from dealers, often banks, which make markets in the securities. Historically, these quotes were accessed via phone, but they increasingly are disseminated using electronic chat, such as Symphony or Bloomberg, or electronic request-for-quote platforms. Just as it was before the onset of these electronic platforms, dealers do not provide quotes continuously; they provide them only on request. There is limited algorithmic trading in bond markets, except for on-the-run, or most recently issued, US Treasuries in benchmark maturities and bond and interest rate futures contracts.
rationales.B: Fixed income has limited transparency and limited electronic trading. Dealers quote only on request and most individual bonds trade infrequently, so there is no continuous, fully electronic market across the asset class.
rationales.C: Fixed income and equities differ substantially. Equities are exchange traded with high pre- and post-trade transparency and well-established algorithmic trading, whereas fixed income is dealer-intermediated with quotes supplied only on request.

questions.stem: In fixed-income markets, small trades and large, urgent trades are most likely implemented through:

options.A: algorithmic trading.
options.B: broker risk trades via requests for quote.
options.C: automated execution with no trader involvement.

rationales.A: There is limited algorithmic trading in bond markets, confined mainly to on-the-run US Treasuries in benchmark maturities and to bond and interest rate futures contracts. The combination of illiquidity and infrequent trading creates challenges for algorithmic trading across the rest of the asset class.
rationales.B: Small trades and large, urgent trades are usually implemented through broker risk trades, via requests for quote, where the broker acts as the counterparty and takes the contract into inventory, because the securities are hard to source otherwise. Large, non-urgent trades are generally implemented using a high-touch approach, with brokers acting as agents to source liquidity, which makes them agency trades instead of principal trades.
rationales.C: High-touch, trader-intermediated execution remains important in fixed income. Sourcing a bond generally requires a broker either to commit capital as principal or to work the order as an agent, so execution without trader involvement is not the norm.

questions.stem: Exchange-traded derivatives (futures, options) most likely have:

options.A: fully customized contracts only.
options.B: high transparency and standardized contracts.
options.C: no market transparency at all.

rationales.A: Exchange-traded futures and options are highly standardized contracts, not customized ones; fewer than 1,000 liquid and highly standardized contracts are outstanding. Customization is the province of the OTC derivative markets.
rationales.B: Similar to exchange-traded equities, market transparency is high and trade price, size, quote, and depth of book data are publicly available. Contracts are liquid and highly standardized, with fewer than 1,000 outstanding. Electronic trading is widespread for exchange-traded derivatives; however, algorithmic trading is not as evolved as in equity markets and is currently used more for trading in futures than in options. Large, urgent trades sweep the book, large, non-urgent trades use algorithms, and the buy side generally uses direct market access for small trades.
rationales.C: Transparency is high on derivative exchanges. Trade price, size, quote and depth of book data are publicly available, much as they are for exchange-traded equities.

questions.stem: OTC derivative markets most likely have:

options.A: no dealer involvement in trade execution.
options.B: transparency comparable to listed equity markets.
options.C: historical opacity now reduced by regulation.

rationales.A: Trading OTC derivatives takes place through dealers, which makes dealer intermediation central to the market's structure. That intermediation is precisely what the post-crisis reforms set out to illuminate, not something the market does without.
rationales.B: Historical opacity is the defining feature of OTC derivative markets, with little public data about prices, trade sizes and structure details. That is the opposite of the pre- and post-trade transparency of listed equity markets, and it is why Dodd-Frank and the G-20 agenda pushed transparency onto these markets through swap data repositories.
rationales.C: OTC derivative markets have historically been opaque, with little public data about prices, trade sizes, and structure details. Regulatory efforts have focused on increasing transparency and reducing counterparty risk in these markets: the G-20 agreement of 2009 and, in the United States, the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act, enacted in 2010, which significantly increased post-trade transparency with the establishment of swap data repositories (SDRs) to which trade details must be submitted, together with central clearing for standardized derivatives. Trading still takes place through dealers. Large, urgent trades are implemented as broker risk trades and large, non-urgent trades through a high-touch agency approach, and large customized trades often require a strong price concession to find a buyer or seller.

questions.stem: Spot foreign exchange (currency) markets are most likely:

options.A: entirely over-the-counter.
options.B: regulated under a single global cross-border framework.
options.C: centrally cleared and regulated.

rationales.A: There is no exchange or centralized clearing place for the majority of spot foreign exchange, or currency, trades. Spot currency markets consist of a number of electronic venues and broker markets, and the currency market is an entirely OTC market. The structure is multi-tiered: the interbank market sits at the top level, with large international banks and financial firms acting as dealers, followed by small and medium-sized banks and institutions, and then commercial companies and retail traders. Daily volume is often more than $1 trillion.
rationales.B: Despite being a global market, spot FX has almost no cross-border regulation. There is no single global framework governing it and no mandatory consolidated trade reporting of the kind found in regulated exchange markets.
rationales.C: The majority of spot FX trades are not centrally cleared. There is no exchange or centralized clearing place for them, and regulation of the market, particularly across borders, is minimal.

questions.stem: In spot FX markets, large, urgent trades are most likely implemented through:

options.A: requests for quote to multiple competing dealers.
options.B: a single pre-designated dealer.
options.C: a central clearinghouse.

rationales.A: Electronic trading in currencies has grown substantially over the years in parallel with algorithmic trading strategies of equities. For large, urgent trades, requests for quote are generally submitted to multiple dealers competing for a trade. Large, non-urgent trades are mostly executed using algorithms, such as TWAP, or a high-touch agency approach, and small trades are usually implemented using direct market access.
rationales.B: Routing a large, urgent trade to one dealer forgoes the competition that a request for quote sent to several dealers creates. Multiple dealers compete for urgent trades, and that competition is what improves the price the trader obtains.
rationales.C: Spot FX has no central clearing. There is no exchange or centralized clearing place for the majority of spot currency trades, which settle bilaterally in an entirely OTC market.

questions.curriculum_ref: Comparison of Markets — FX trade implementation

questions.stem: For a large, non-urgent sell of OTC options, the most appropriate execution approach is most likely:

options.A: Closing auction.
options.B: Algorithmic execution.
options.C: Broker agency trade.

rationales.A: OTC options are not exchange-traded, so there is no exchange closing auction in which the position could be sold. A closing auction is a venue for listed securities, where an exchange crosses accumulated buy and sell interest at a single closing price.
rationales.B: OTC options are not typically traded algorithmically. Algorithms work an order against continuous, electronically accessible liquidity, which customized bilateral contracts do not have; there is no central order book for an algorithm to slice the order into.
rationales.C: A large, non-urgent sell of OTC options generally involves a broker agency trade, in which the broker acts on behalf of the manager to find a matching buyer for the options. Because the order is non-urgent, the manager can give the broker time to search out that counterparty rather than demand immediate liquidity. Depending on the level of contract customization, however, a significant price concession may still be required by the manager to complete order execution, since customization limits the pool of investors for whom the contract terms are a good fit.

questions.stem: For a large, urgent sell of corporate bonds, the most appropriate execution is most likely:

options.A: Algorithmic execution.
options.B: Broker risk trade.
options.C: Closing auction.

rationales.A: Algorithmic execution is limited for corporate bonds. The market is dealer-based and fragmented across many individual issues, so there is not enough continuous electronic liquidity in a single bond for an algorithm to work a large order, least of all an urgent one.
rationales.B: A large, urgent sell of corporate bonds would usually involve a broker risk trade via the request-for-quote process. Because of corporate bond illiquidity, the likelihood of finding a matching buyer is low. For more immediate (urgent) order execution, a broker would be needed to act as counterparty to the trade, taking the bonds and their associated risk into inventory. That transfer of risk to the broker is what makes it a risk trade rather than an agency trade, and the broker is compensated for it through the quoted price.
rationales.C: Corporate bonds do not trade on stock exchanges, so no exchange closing auction exists in which to sell them. Corporate bond trading takes place over the counter between dealers and clients, typically through a request-for-quote process.

drills.los_text: explain how trade costs are measured and determine the cost of a trade

questions.stem: The implementation shortfall (IS) metric is most likely:

options.A: The paper portfolio return minus the actual portfolio return.
options.B: The firm's total commission expense over the period.
options.C: The ex ante estimate of an order's expected trading cost.

rationales.A: The implementation shortfall metric is the most important ex post trade cost measurement used in finance, because it gives portfolio managers the total cost associated with implementing the investment decision. IS = Paper portfolio return − Actual portfolio return. The notional or paper portfolio is one in which all transactions are assumed to take place at the manager's decision price, while the actual return reflects realized transactions, including all fees and costs. The gap between the two is everything implementation cost the manager.
rationales.B: Commissions are only one component of implementation shortfall, and they sit inside the fixed fees term alongside exchange fees and taxes. Implementation shortfall spans the full difference between the paper portfolio's return and the actual portfolio's return, which also captures execution cost on the shares filled and opportunity cost on the shares left unexecuted.
rationales.C: Implementation shortfall is measured ex post, after the fact, against the manager's decision price. A pre-trade estimate of the cost an order is expected to incur is a separate, ex ante exercise used to plan the trade and select an execution strategy; it is not a measurement of what the trade actually cost.

questions.stem: Implementation shortfall is most likely decomposed into:

options.A: Execution cost, opportunity cost, and fixed fees.
options.B: Delay cost, trading cost, and opportunity cost.
options.C: Commissions, market impact, and spread cost.

rationales.A: The implementation shortfall formulation decomposes the total cost of the trade into three categories: execution cost, opportunity cost, and fixed fees. Execution cost corresponds to the shares that were transacted in the market, and captures the difference between the prices actually paid and the decision price. Opportunity cost corresponds to the unexecuted shares of the order; it is the cost associated with not being able to transact the entire order at the manager's decision price and is due to adverse price movement over the trading period. The fixed fees component includes all explicit fees, such as commissions, exchange fees, and taxes.
rationales.B: Delay cost and trading cost come from Wagner's expanded implementation shortfall, which splits the execution cost component in two so that managers can see where in the implementation cycle the cost arose. This triad also omits fixed fees altogether. The basic decomposition is execution cost, opportunity cost, and fixed fees.
rationales.C: Commissions belong inside the fixed fees component, and market impact and bid–ask spread are drivers of execution cost rather than categories of their own. None of the three named here is one of the three implementation shortfall categories.

questions.stem: An order to buy 1,000 shares of Impulse Robotics is placed at a decision price of £10.00; 700 shares are filled at £10.07, the stock closes at £10.08, and fees total £14. The execution cost of the order is closest to:

rationales.A: Execution cost is calculated as the difference between the cost of the real portfolio and the cost of the paper portfolio, and reflects the execution price paid for the amount of shares in the order actually filled: (700 × £10.07) − (700 × £10.00) = £7,049 − £7,000 = £49. Only the 700 filled shares enter this component, because unfilled shares never transacted at a market price.
rationales.B: £14 is the fixed fees component of implementation shortfall: the explicit commissions, exchange fees, and taxes paid on the order. Fixed fees are incurred regardless of where the shares printed relative to the decision price, so they are not part of execution cost.
rationales.C: £24 is the opportunity cost: (1,000 − 700) × (£10.08 − £10.00), the 300 unexecuted shares valued at the adverse move from the decision price to the closing price. It measures the cost of not completing the order, so it belongs to a different component than execution cost, which applies only to the 700 shares actually filled. Total implementation shortfall here is £49 + £24 + £14 = £87, or 87 bps of the £10,000 paper portfolio.
